full_judgment:
5. In all 14 witnesses were examined by the prosecution in support of the prosecution case, while the defence examined no witness. The learned District and Session Judge, Manikganj, on hearing the parties and considering the evidence on record, found the accused guilty under section 302 of the Penal Code and sentenced him to life imprisonment. 

 7. Mr. Shaukat Ali, Khan, the learned Advocate appearing for the accused-appellant submits that the order of conviction is wholly illegal as the same is not supported by any evidence. Mr. Khan argues that there is no evidence to connect the accused with the alleged commission of murder. The learned Judge convicted the accused without any legal evidence and as such the accused is entitled to be acquitted. 

 8. Mr. A.K.M. Shamsul Karim, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing for the state, on the otherhand, submits that prosecution successfully proved the guilt of the accused by circumstantial evidence. Mr. Karim also argued that the judgment and order of conviction is founded on legal evidence and as such is sustainable in law. 

 23. P.W. 14 is the Investigating Officer, M.A. Rashid. who stated in his deposition that he went to the place of occurrence on 6.12.85, prepared inquest report, examined the witnesses, sent the dead body to hospital for post mortem examination through Constable Abdul Karim and Muslem Ali, seized certain articles, made the seizure list and after due investigation, submitted the charge-sheet. He stated that one Joynal Abedin, member of Dharala Union Parishad, filed a written application and informed him about the occurrence and he made a G.D. entry in the general diary register. He admitted that in the eye of law this application containing information could be treated as an F.I.R., but as doubt might arise, he accepted the first information report after entering that G.D. entry in the general diary register. These are the evidence adduced by the prosecution in support of the prosecution case. The learned District and Sessions Judge found complete and strong chain of circumstances which according to him are reasonable to arrive at the conclusion that the accused Mohasin out of enemity and grudge inflicted multiple cut and bleeding injures with sharp cutting weapons on the person of victim Jalal with the help of his associates and thus accused Mohasin committed the murder of victim Jalal Khan and as such is liable for commission of the offence under section 302 of the Penal Code. 

 24. Let us now consider the evidence on record to see if the order of conviction passed by the learned Sessions Judge is sustainable in law or not. We have seen that P.W. 1 Suraiya Begum, P.W. 2, Bhetku Mia, P.W. 3 Korban Kazi, P.W. 4 Mujibur Rahman, P.W, 5 Nazrul Islam, P.W. 6 Humayun Kabir and P.W. 12 Golam Moula have stated in their statements that the deceased Jalaluddin Khan was first seen at Joymondap Bazar and thereafter he was found at Bhum dakhin Bazar at about 7 to 7-30 P.M. They also stated to have seen Mohasin purchasing some Biris at Bhakum Bazar. Prosecution witness No. 2 further stated that deceased Jalal Khan went towards the south and accused Mohasin also was found to have gone towards the south though there is time gap in between their departure and none said a word that the two ever met together at any point of time or at any place. Further prosecution tried to prove by evidence of P.Ws. 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 12 the existence of enemity and litigations between deceased Jalal and father of the accused Mohasin over the landed properties and some fisheries. Prosecution has also tried to prove the presence of accused Mohasin with some unknown persons near about the graveyard by the side of which the dead body of Jalaluddin was found on the day following. No eye-witness is forthwith coming to say that accused Mohasin had met the deceased or committed any act which may be called an offence under the Penal Code. No person has heard any cry or sound of alarm from that particular area or that the I.O. has found any marks of violence near the place of occurrence or any blood stained earth was recovered from there so as to suggest that a murder took place there. The evidence of the prosecution witnesses at best could prove the existence of enemity and a suspicion may occur in our mind. But too many people went to Roy Dakhin Bazar on that day. It is not uncommon in our country to substitute a person with whom the informant party has enemity for the real culprit in order to satisfy the grudge. Suspicion, however strong may that be, that cannot be a substitute for legal evidence. Where there is total absence of physical circumstances to connect the accused with the crime, and there is a back ground of strong enemity, the ocular evidence must come from unimpeachable source. Furthermore, howsoever a judge may morally be convinced as the truth of a particular fact, he must not act upon it in basing his decision or conclusion without being supported by any legal evidence. For, moral conviction is of no value and can never form the foundation of a fact proved. The learned Judge must bear in mind that his capricious and reckless thought has no bearing on an issue which needs be proved only by legal evidence and surmises and conjectures have no role to play. Examination of large number of witnesses may be an impressive one but that does not invest the court with the power to convict the accused on mere surmises and conjectures in place of any legal proof. The learned fudge has travelled far beyond the scope of his limit and power and acted capriciously and in an irresponsible manner to convict the accused-appellant under section 302 of the Penal Code. The learned Judge has based his decision on Ext. 3, a statement made by the prosecution witnesses No.3 and 12 before a Magistrate. But on a careful scrutiny of Ext. 3, it appears that it has not been written and recorded in accordance with normal procedure. Even there is no seal or signature of the recording Magistrate in Ext. 3. The Magistrate has not been examined. No one has proved the Ext. 3. In our view this Ext. 3 is not at all admissible in evidence and as such Ext. 3 is excluded from our consideration. The learned District Judge and Sessions Judge against the weight of evidence and contrary to the statements of the prosecution witnesses concluded to the effect that: " 

 "In the light of my findings and observations made above on the basis of a proper scrutiny of documentary and oral evidences on record, I find a complete and strong chain of circumstances to believe, with no other reasonable alternative to come to a conclusion that accused Mohasin, out of previous enemity and grudge, inflicted multiple cut and bleeding injures with sharp cutting weapons upon the persons of victim Jalal Khan with the help of his associates, whose recognition has not been fully established for want of corroborative evidence, and thereby, he committed the murder of victim Jalal Khan by intentionally causing his death as confirmed by the post mortem report Ext. 8, proved by medical officer P.W. 11 Dr. Shushil Kumar Mondal." 

 In utter surprise we are constrained to note that no witness has ever stated or uttered a single word as to inflicting of injuries not to speak of multiple cut and bleeding injuries with sharp cutting weapon on the person of the victim with the help of his associates anywhere throughout their depositions. If the findings of the learned Judge be based on no evidence or on misinterpretation of evidence or the same be perverse resulting in miscarriage of justice, and the findings are based on certain prejudiced impressions or prior assumptions of the learned Judge who looks upon every piece of simple and straight evidence with considerable skepticism in order to base his conviction or leads to the conclusion with such based skepticism, the conviction is liable to be set aside.
